content: Bristol-Myers Squibb, commonly referred to as BMS, is a pharmaceutical company that was established in 1989 through the merger of two companies: Bristol-Myers Company, founded in 1887 by William McLaren Bristol and John Ripley Myers in Clinton, New York, and E.R. Squibb Corporation. The company is headquartered in New York City. Peter R. Dolan, who served as the Chairman and CEO, was dismissed in September 2006 due to his handling of a patent dispute involving the drug Plavix. He was replaced by James Cornelius, who initially served as interim CEO but later assumed the permanent role of CEO and Chairman following the retirement of James Robinson III. Robinson had been appointed Chairman as part of a settlement related to a channel-stuffing scandal. This scandal, along with others in the 2000s, severely impacted the company and led to over $1 billion in state and federal fines. To avoid federal prosecution, Bristol-Myers Squibb was placed under the oversight of a federal judge, and former FBI director Louis Freeh was appointed to the Board of Directors for a two-year period. Additionally, Richard Lane, the former head of the pharmaceutical group, and Fred Schiff, the former CFO, were indicted for federal securities violations. The company’s primary research and development facilities are located in Lawrenceville, New Jersey (formerly Squibb) and Wallingford, Connecticut (formerly Bristol-Myers), with additional sites in the United States, Ireland, and other countries. This restructuring has involved layoffs, outsourcing, and offshoring operations, with a notable shift of research and development activities to lower-cost locations such as India and China. In 2005, Bristol-Myers Squibb was one of 53 entities that contributed the maximum allowable amount of $250,000 to the second inauguration of President George W. Bush. The company is listed on the Fortune 500, ranking 129th in 2007. Bristol-Myers Squibb produces prescription pharmaceuticals and healthcare products across various therapeutic areas. It is also the parent company of Mead Johnson, which manufactures nutritional products like Enfamil baby formula and Tri-Vi-Sol infant vitamin supplements, as well as ConvaTec, a global leader in ostomy and wound care products. The company’s stated mission is to Extend and Enhance Human Life by addressing unmet medical needs. Lance Armstrong, a testicular cancer survivor who was treated with Bristol-Myers Squibb medication, has appeared in several of the company’s marketing campaigns. Key Pharmaceutical Products Bristol-Myers Squibb manufactures a range of pharmaceutical products, including: Abilify (aripiprazole): An antipsychotic medication. ATRIPLA (efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate): A combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV. Avalide (irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide): A medication for hypertension. Avapro (irbesartan): An angiotensin receptor blocker for hypertension. Baraclude (entecavir): An antiviral drug for hepatitis B. Cardiolite: A diagnostic agent for myocardial perfusion imaging. Erbitux (cetuximab): A monoclonal antibody for cancer treatment. Ixempra (ixabepilone): A chemotherapy agent. Orencia (abatacept): A biologic for autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. Plavix (clopidogrel bisulfate): An antiplatelet medication. Pravachol (pravastatin sodium): A statin for cholesterol management. Reyataz (atazanavir sulfate): An antiretroviral for HIV. Sprycel (dasatinib): A tyrosine kinase inhibitor for leukemia. Sustiva (efavirenz): An antiretroviral for HIV. Taxol (paclitaxel): A chemotherapy drug. Videx EC (didanosine): An antiretroviral for HIV. Zerit (stavudine): An antiretroviral for HIV. Taxol (Paclitaxel) Bristol-Myers Squibb once held the exclusive contract to harvest the bark of endangered yew trees in the United States for the production of paclitaxel (Taxol), a chemotherapy drug. Current production of paclitaxel now relies on renewable sources. Although BMS originally held the license for paclitaxel, the drug is now produced by multiple generic manufacturers. Products Under Development The company is actively developing several new pharmaceutical products, including: Ipilimumab: A monoclonal antibody for cancer immunotherapy. Belatacept: A biologic for organ transplant rejection prevention. Saxagliptin: A medication for type 2 diabetes. Apixaban: An anticoagulant. Pexacerfont: A drug targeting stress-related disorders. Dapagliflozin: A medication for type 2 diabetes. Scandals and Allegations On June 30, 1999, consumer advocate Ralph Nader testified before the House Budget Committee, highlighting that the development of Taxol was largely funded by the federal government, while Bristol-Myers Squibb retained production rights, with potential annual earnings exceeding $1 billion. In 2002, the company was implicated in an accounting scandal involving the improper booking of sales through channel-stuffing, a practice where excess inventory is offered to customers to inflate sales figures. This led to a significant restatement of revenues for the years 1999–2001. Bristol-Myers Squibb settled with the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission, agreeing to pay $150 million without admitting or denying guilt. The company also faced lawsuits from state attorneys general seeking monetary damages. In July 2006, a criminal investigation into the company became public, and the FBI raided its corporate offices. The investigation focused on the distribution of Plavix and allegations of collusion. On September 12, 2006, a federal monitor, former Judge Frederick B. Lacey, recommended the removal of CEO Peter Dolan due to his handling of the Plavix dispute. Later that day, the company announced Dolan’s resignation. Under James Cornelius’s leadership, all executives involved in the channel-stuffing and generic competition scandals have since left the company. The most recent departure was Andrew Bodner, Executive Vice President, who was indicted for his role in the Plavix-Apotex case.
